question.text: A copper processor needs 100 MT of copper in 3 months. Current spot: Rs 750/kg, 3-month futures: Rs 770/kg. The 3-month cost of carry (financing + storage + insurance) is Rs 10/kg, and the processor's convenience yield for holding physical copper is Rs 30/kg. Based on F = S + C - Y, should the processor buy spot or futures to minimize effective cost?

answer.text: Buy in spot market - the effective spot cost (750 + 10 - 30 = Rs 730/kg) is below the futures price of Rs 770/kg
Buy futures at Rs 770 - it is always cheaper than spot ownership
Wait for prices to fall further before buying
Buy half in spot and half in futures for diversification

explanation.text: The Logic: Using the cost-of-carry relation F = S + C - Y, the processor's effective cost of holding spot for 3 months is 750 + 10 (carry) - 30 (convenience yield) = Rs 730/kg, which is below the Rs 770/kg futures price. Because the processor actually uses copper in production, the convenience yield is a real benefit (no production stoppages), so buying spot is the lower-cost option. The Trap: "Futures always cheaper" ignores convenience yield; "wait for prices to fall" is speculation, not a hedging decision; the 50:50 split is an arbitrary diversification rule, not a cost-minimisation strategy. The audit flagged the original because the 3-month carry cost C was not stated - without C, the spot-vs-futures choice was indeterminate (buying spot is only supported when C is below about Rs 50/kg). Note: The original was ambiguous because the 3-month carry cost C was missing. The stem now states C = Rs 10/kg explicitly, and references the F = S + C - Y formula from NISM Series-XVI (December 2025), pp.54-55, making "buy in spot market" the uniquely supported answer.
